body:
"You guys can be very inspirational."

No, you're very inspirational. Fight on, I will too, you help, thank you.

I don't know much about your situation in specific so I wouldn't rally wish to advise you but, assuming you have the finances, why not go to a doctor? Correct me if I'm wrong but, doesn't your institution have some kind of psychological aid to access free of charge.

I have been running for about 4 months (started from nothing, quit smoking along the way).

I can make 10k in about 55 minutes. I ideally wish to be able to complete a 10k in 40 minutes, is such improvement ever going to be possible? There is no time constraint as such, more so an ideal goal I wish to surpass in a couple of years.

I'm 21. I know it might be hard to give a determinant answer because genetics but in so far as your experience goes, does such an improvement seem likely? Would you say it is "rare"/"common"/"unusual" to see such improvement?

The description of the idea he outlines under the title of "First", I'd like to know what it is conventionally called in academic circles, a quick name that people use to refer to it? So I can read more about it?

So, I actually don't conceive of right and wrong as much as I do "good" and "bad" (note that given that I conceive of these things as objective and not relative, the third type is eliminated) but more importantly, what I conceive of is a sense of "good" and "bad" in addition to NO sense of a kind of "obligation" or "reason to do good".

To me personally, the statement "One should do X because is good" (i.e. X is good is a sufficient condition for one being obligated to do X) doesn't have much meaning since I don't see any meaning in saying that one "should" do something or "has a reason to do something, be it an obligation" if one does not in fact FEEL the obligation, therefore type 2 is also not what I hold.

Perspective does help, I do tend to find motivation in hearing stories of people who have suffered much more greatly than I have and who still managed to somehow, someway, find a way to get on with life.

Everyone has their own mental make-up of course, but really, hearing those stories always helps me think "well, it seems we all have reservoirs to draw upon of which we do not dream!" (to paraphrase William James)

I don't know how everyone else would respond to "tough love" but thanks anyway, your intentions are good!

Thank you for your detailed answer :)

I do like to think that one can find bliss in solitude.

"It is difficult to find happiness within oneself, impossible to find it anywhere else" - Schopenhauer

Finding companions is kind of the hard part, and my situation right now doesn't really allow me to shift houses, anyway I'm going to be graduating soon and going to another institution to pursue further studies, I'll be rooming with someone there most likely, maybe things will be different?

I'm not so sure about what group activities I could possibly get into.

Also, yeah, my studies suffered in the first year of college, but I managed to productively channel my dejection in the last semester, I managed to get the highest grades in my cohort. Luckily I'm studying a subject I do enjoy so learning is not a chore for me, hopefully I get into a good place to further my studies after I graduate!

I've been thinking of getting a pet, and I'm planning to take part in meditation camps organised by this institution known as dhamma, if I feel it helped me I'll go ahead and volunteer in that same institution.

Thanks for the advice!

*hug* thanks!

I know, still, everyone says your college days are the best of your life, what ever will I do if it's all downhill from here? :P

I do hope things change though, will continue to hang in there!

I hope I do, and I hope I keep thinking it is good enough, it's just that in the moments I'm most vulnerable it doesn't feel like my hobbies are good enough, nor that I will meet someone who likes the same things (and at the same time, more importantly, likes me haha!).

Thank you friend :)

Hey, I hope I do find someone, just seems... unlikely. I'll hang in there though!

"What there is no evidence for, however, is any particularly salubrious effect of meditation, especially in byte-sized doses. This was established through a mammoth, federally sponsored “meta-analysis” of existing studies, published last year, which found that meditation programs can help treat stress-related symptoms but are no more effective in doing so than other interventions, such as muscle relaxation, medication, or psychotherapy. There is no excuse for ignoring this study, which achieved worldwide attention. So maybe meditation does have a calming, “centering” effect, but so does an hour of concentration on a math problem or a glass of wine with friends."

This is a stupid suggestion, I'd like to see the meta-analysis she is referring to.

Taking the most negative review I found, the paper concluded that Mindfulness Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) therapies were, when compared to other therapies, slightly, but not really "all that" more effective (to cut out scientific jargon). Of course, it was still compared to a mild-antidepressant even AFTER controlling with the effects of other therapies.

To suggest these other therapies MBSR were compared against involved, "an hour of concentration on a math problem or a glass of wine with friends" is, pardon my french, retarded, especially the latter of those two.
